ch5n1.title: A smell in the dark

questions.q: There is no signpost. How do the two animals know they have found the right way home?

options.text: A little feeling inside them says the track leads home.
options.why: Clue: "that small inquiring something which all animals carry inside them" says "Yes, quite right; this leads home!"

options.text: The Otter drew them a map of the track before he went back.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 never mentions a map. The Otter isn't with them any more.

options.text: They follow the church bells ringing from the village ahead.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 says they "heard the sheep", not bells. Look at what tells them the track is right.

options.text: they asked sheep
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: they walked towards the sheep, but nobody asked them anything. Something inside the animals told them.

questions.q: How can we tell the Mole isn't keen to go through the village?

options.text: He slows down and sounds unsure, as animals don't like villages.
options.why: Clue: he speaks "somewhat dubiously, slackening his pace", and "The animals did not hold with villages".

options.text: He sits down in the road and refuses to walk one more step.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 2 he only slows down. He keeps walking all the way through the village.

options.text: He says the people in the village once chased him with a big stick.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole says only one thing in paragraph 2, and it isn't about being chased.

options.text: he slows down
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Most of the cottage windows were *innocent of blinds*. What does that mean?

options.text: The windows had no blinds, so anyone could see right inside.
options.why: Clue: the lookers-in can see the people "gathered round the tea-table". Innocent of here means without.

options.text: The blinds had done nothing wrong, so nobody could blame them at all.
options.why: Clue check: blinds can't be naughty! Paragraph 4 is about how easily the animals can see into the rooms.

options.text: The windows were brand new and nobody had ever looked through them.
options.why: Clue check: the animals are looking through them right now, watching "a cat being stroked".

options.text: no blinds up
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: In the village, the animals feel cosy watching the cottages. What snaps them out of it and reminds them how far from home they are?

options.text: A sting of icy sleet wakes them up, cold, tired and far from home.
options.why: Clue: "a small sting of frozen sleet on the skin woke them as from a dream, and they knew their toes to be cold".

options.text: A big dog barks from a cottage and chases them right out of the village.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 says the dogs are "safe indoors". Nobody chases them.

options.text: The bird in the cage wakes up and starts singing very loudly at them.
options.why: Clue check: the bird only yawns and goes back to sleep. Look at what hits them "in the back of the neck".

options.text: icy sleet
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Why doesn't the Rat notice when something suddenly happens to the Mole?

options.text: He is walking ahead with his eyes fixed on the road in front.
options.why: Clue: the Rat "was walking a little way ahead... his eyes fixed on the straight grey road in front of him".

options.text: He is fast asleep on his feet after the long day out with Otter.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 6 says he is walking with his eyes fixed on the road. He's awake.

options.text: He has gone back to the village to have one more look at the bird.
options.why: Clue check: they have left the village behind. Paragraph 6 starts "Once beyond the village".

options.text: Rat is deaf
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 6 tells us where the Rat is walking and where he is looking.

questions.q: The summons *took him like an electric shock*. What does that mean?

options.text: Something hit the Mole so suddenly it made him jump inside.
options.why: Clue: it happens "suddenly", and in paragraph 7 he "stopped dead in his tracks" and tingled "through and through".

options.text: The Mole touched a wire by the road and it gave him a real shock.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 7 says it was a smell, "one of these mysterious fairy calls". No wires!

options.text: Lightning struck the road right beside the Mole and made him jump.
options.why: Clue check: there is no storm. It is a smell that reaches him in paragraph 7.

options.text: a big surprise
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: At first the Mole can't remember what the smell is. What does he realise a moment later, and how does it seem to feel about him?

options.text: It is his old home, and it misses him and wants him back.
options.why: Clue: "Home!" and the home "was missing him, and wanted him back, and was telling him so, through his nose".

options.text: It is the Rat's supper cooking, and it makes him feel very hungry indeed.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole was thinking about supper in paragraph 6, but paragraph 8 starts with a different word. What is it?

options.text: It is Badger's house nearby, and Badger is calling him inside.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 8 says it is "his old home that he had hurriedly forsaken". Whose home is that?

options.text: his old home
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The home calls to him *sorrowfully, reproachfully, but with no bitterness or anger*. How does the home seem to feel?

options.text: It is sad and a bit hurt that he left, but it is not cross.
options.why: Clue: sorrowfully means sadly, reproachfully means a little hurt, and "no bitterness or anger" means not cross.

options.text: It is furious with the Mole and wants to punish him for leaving.
options.why: Clue check: the quote itself says "no bitterness or anger". Furious is very angry.

options.text: It is happy he has a new life and hopes he never comes back.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 8 says the home "wanted him back".

options.text: very angry
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: read the end of the quote again: "no bitterness or anger".

questions.q: Which word best describes the Mole when the smell reaches him, and what is your proof?

options.text: Homesick: he begs the Rat to stop, as he must go to his old home.
options.why: Clue: "It's my home, my old home!... And I must go to it, I must, I must!"

options.text: Bored: he yawns and says he would much rather stay in the village.
options.why: Clue check: it's the little bird in paragraph 5 that yawns, not the Mole.

options.text: Angry: he shouts that he never wants to see the Rat again.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 11 he says "Please, please come back!" He wants the Rat with him.

options.text: Lazy: he sits on a tree stump and won't walk one more step.
options.why: Clue check: there are no tree stumps tonight. The Mole is standing on the road, calling.

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: On the dark road, begging the Rat to come back, desperate to go home.
options.why: Clue: "pleaded the poor Mole, in anguish of heart" and "Oh, come back, Ratty! Please, please come back!"

options.text: In the village, happily watching a little bird asleep in its warm cage.
options.why: Clue check: they left the village in paragraph 6. The last paragraph is out on the road.

options.text: At Mole End already, dusting his old things and feeling very proud.
options.why: Clue check: in the last paragraph he hasn't reached his home yet. He is still begging the Rat to stop.

options.text: fast asleep
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 11 the Mole is calling out. Is that asleep?

hints: The Rat is too far ahead to hear, so the Mole follows him sadly until he bursts into tears.
The Mole runs off alone to find his home, but he gets lost until the Rat tracks his footprints.
The Rat hears the Mole at last, so they follow the smell together and find the old home.
Snow starts to fall and hides the smell, but the Mole digs down until he finds his tunnel.

ch5n2.title: Following the nose

questions.q: At the start of tonight the Rat can smell something too. What is it, and why does it make him hurry on?

options.text: He smells snow and isn't sure of the way, so he won't stop.
options.why: Clue: he smells "something suspiciously like approaching snow", then says "the snow's coming on again, and I'm not sure of the way!"

options.text: He smells his supper cooking back home, so he runs off to eat it.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 says he was "much taken up with the weather". What weather can he smell?

options.text: He smells the Wild Wood animals nearby, so he wants to hide.
options.why: Clue check: nobody mentions the Wild Wood tonight. Look at the end of paragraph 1.

options.text: snow is coming
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Mole stands alone with *his heart torn asunder*. What does that mean?

options.text: He feels pulled two ways, between his old home and his friend.
options.why: Clue: the smells of home "pleaded" with him, but "his loyalty to his friend stood firm". Torn asunder means pulled apart.

options.text: His heart is broken into pieces and a doctor will have to mend it.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole walks on down the road straight afterwards. This is about feelings, not a real heart.

options.text: Somebody has torn his coat so his chest is showing in the cold.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 says nothing about his coat. It's about the "big sob gathering" inside him.

options.text: pulled two ways
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Mole wants his home very badly. Why does he follow the Rat instead?

options.text: He is loyal and would never dream of leaving his friend alone.
options.why: Clue: "his loyalty to his friend stood firm. Never for a moment did he dream of abandoning him."

options.text: He is frightened of the dark and does not dare to go on his own.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 gives the real reason, and it's about his friend, not the dark.

options.text: The Rat has his arm, so the Mole cannot get away from him.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat is "very far ahead" in paragraph 1. He isn't holding the Mole at all yet.

options.text: he's loyal
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How can we tell the Rat has no idea how sad the Mole is on the walk?

options.text: He chats about fires and supper, not noticing Mole's silence.
options.why: Clue: he "began chattering cheerfully about... what a supper he meant to eat; never noticing his companion's silence".

options.text: He asks the Mole why he is crying and the Mole says it's the cold.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 4 the Rat never asks. He only notices the Mole is tired much later.

options.text: He sings a happy song all the way and makes the Mole join in.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 4 says the Rat is chattering, not singing, and the Mole is silent.

options.text: Rat is sleepy
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 4 the Rat is chattering away. What is he not noticing?

questions.q: The Mole cries because *he had lost what he could hardly be said to have found*. What does that mean?

options.text: He only just smelt his home, and now he has lost it again.
options.why: Clue: he had only caught the smell of home on the road, then had to leave it behind. He hardly found it before it was gone.

options.text: He found a lost coin on the road and then dropped it again.
options.why: Clue check: nobody finds a coin. Think about what the Mole smelt on the road in paragraph 3.

options.text: He has lost his way home to the river and nobody can find him.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat is sitting right beside him on the tree stumps. He isn't lost.

options.text: lost his map
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: there is no map. What did the Mole find, only for a moment, on the road?

questions.q: Early on, the Rat says they mustn't stop. What does he call himself once the Mole explains, and why?

options.text: A pig, as he wouldn't listen when the Mole begged to stop.
options.why: Clue: after the Mole sobs "you wouldn't turn back, Ratty", the Rat says "What a pig I have been!"

options.text: A hero, because he got the Mole home safely through the snow.
options.why: Clue check: they aren't home yet, and the Rat isn't proud of himself in paragraph 9 at all.

options.text: A fool, because he got them both lost on the dark road again.
options.why: Clue check: nobody is lost. Read the word the Rat uses in paragraph 9.

options.text: a plain pig
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence, and say why he feels that way. Which option does it properly?

questions.q: The Rat gets up *remarking carelessly* that they'd better be getting on. Does he really not care?

options.text: He does care; he acts casual so Mole won't guess his plan.
options.why: Clue: he sets off "over the toilsome way they had come", back towards Mole's home. The careless voice hides a kind surprise.

options.text: No, he has stopped caring and just wants to get home to bed.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 10 says he walks back "the way they had come". That's away from his own bed!

options.text: He is careless, so he drops the Mole's things all over the road.
options.why: Clue check: nothing is dropped. Look at which way the Rat walks in paragraph 10.

options.text: a surprise plan
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: It is dark and they can't see much. How does the Rat know the Mole has caught the smell again?

options.text: He feels a thrill run down the Mole's arm, linked in his.
options.why: Clue: "the Rat was conscious, through his arm that was linked in Mole's, of a faint sort of electric thrill".

options.text: The Mole shouts "Home!" as loud as he can and starts to cry.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat said "no more talking" in paragraph 15. They move "in silence".

options.text: He sees the Mole's front door shining in the starlight ahead.
options.why: Clue check: the front door is deep underground. They don't see it until the very end.

options.text: Mole sniffs loudly
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the clue too. Clue check: the Rat feels it rather than hears it. Where are their arms?

questions.q: Which word best describes the Rat once he understands, and what is your proof?

options.text: Kind: he turns right round in the snow to help find Mole's home.
options.why: Clue: "I'm going to find this place now, if I stay out all night."

options.text: Grumpy: he tells the Mole off for crying and walks away.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 9 he pats the Mole "gently on the shoulder".

options.text: Selfish: he says his own supper matters more than Mole's old home.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 14 he says "Hang River Bank, and supper too!"

options.text: Scared: he won't follow the Mole down the dark tunnel.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 21 says "the Rat was on the alert, and promptly followed him".

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: Underground at his own front door, glad he found his old home.
options.why: Clue: "directly facing them was Mole's little front door, with 'Mole End' painted" over the bell-pull. His nose led him all the way.

options.text: Still crying on a tree stump by the road, sure he'll never get home.
options.why: Clue check: they left the tree stumps back in paragraph 10. The last paragraph is underground.

options.text: Back at the river bank, eating supper in front of the Rat's fire.
options.why: Clue check: read the name painted over the door in the last paragraph. Whose home is it?

options.text: at River Bank
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: the name painted in the last paragraph is not River Bank.

hints: Mole's home is dusty and bare, so the Rat lights a fire and they tidy it up together.
There seems to be no food in the house, but the Rat hunts through the cupboards until he finds some.
The front door is locked, so the Mole squeezes down the chimney to let the Rat in.
Weasels have moved into Mole End, but the Rat chases them out with his cudgel.

ch5n3.title: Home again

questions.q: How do we know the Mole liked to keep his home neat before he left it?

options.text: He kept a roller so animals couldn't mess up his ground.
options.why: Clue: he "was a tidy animal when at home, could not stand having his ground kicked up", so he kept a roller.

options.text: He hired a gardener to sweep the fore-court every single day.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 never mentions a gardener. Look at what stands on the other side of the door.

options.text: He locked every door so no animal could ever get inside.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 2 the Mole walks straight in. Nothing is locked.

options.text: a tidy animal
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The glass ball *reflected everything all wrong and had a very pleasing effect*. Why is the storyteller being funny?

options.text: It makes everything look silly, yet Mole thinks it's lovely.
options.why: Clue: "all wrong" and "very pleasing" in the same breath. The storyteller is smiling at how much the Mole loves his odd little things.

options.text: It is broken, so Mole wants to throw it out and buy a new one.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 2 Mole's face "beamed at the sight of all these objects so dear to him". He wouldn't throw it out!

options.text: It shows the Mole's face all wrong, so he is scared of it.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole isn't scared. The ball has "a very pleasing effect".

options.text: it's broken
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: nothing is broken. Read the last three words of the quote again.

questions.q: Mole's face beams when he sees the fore-court. A moment later he collapses on a chair. Why does his mood change so fast?

options.text: Inside it's dusty and shabby, and he's ashamed to show Rat.
options.why: Clue: he sees "the dust lying thick on everything" and cries "Why did I bring you to this poor, cold little place".

options.text: Inside, a family of rabbits has moved in and eaten his food.
options.why: Clue check: nobody else is in the house. Look at what the Mole sees in paragraph 2.

options.text: He remembers he has lost his key and can't open the front door.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 2 he "hurried Rat through the door". He's already inside.

options.text: dust everywhere
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: *The Rat paid no heed to his doleful self-reproaches.* Why does the Rat ignore the Mole's moaning?

options.text: He wants to cheer Mole up, so he talks about the good things.
options.why: Clue: straight away he calls out "What a capital little house this is!" He's changing the mood on purpose.

options.text: He cannot hear the Mole, as his ears are full of snow.
options.why: Clue check: nobody's ears are full of snow. Look at what the Rat says instead in paragraph 3.

options.text: He thinks the Mole is right and the house is a dreadful place.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 3 the Rat says "So compact! So well planned!" He doesn't think it's dreadful.

options.text: he is rude
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: read what the Rat calls out in paragraph 3. Is he being rude or kind?

questions.q: How does the Rat work out there must be food somewhere in the house?

options.text: He spots a sardine-opener, so there must be sardines too.
options.why: Clue: "I saw a sardine-opener on the kitchen dresser... that means there are sardines about somewhere". Just like the door-scraper meant a door!

options.text: He smells sausages cooking in the kitchen next door.
options.why: Clue check: nothing is cooking. The sausage is found later, in a drawer, wrapped in silver paper.

options.text: The Mole tells him the cellar is full of bread and butter.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 the Mole groans "No bread! no butter".

options.text: a sardine-opener
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: At first the Mole calls his house a poor, cold little place. What does the Rat keep doing to change how the Mole feels?

options.text: He keeps praising the house and asking about Mole's things.
options.why: Clue: "This is really the jolliest little place I ever was in" and "Tell us all about it, and how you came to make it what it is."

options.text: He tells Mole it's much better than his own house by the river.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat praises Mole End a lot, but he never compares it with his own home.

options.text: He promises to buy Mole a bigger house with lots of new things.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat loves the house just as it is. He never talks about buying anything.

options.text: praises everything
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How can we tell the Rat is very hungry but hides it to be kind?

options.text: He says "wonderful" to Mole's things instead of asking for food.
options.why: Clue: "Rat, who was desperately hungry but strove to conceal it, nodding seriously" and saying "wonderful".

options.text: He sneaks a sardine out of the tin when the Mole isn't looking.
options.why: Clue check: the sardine tin isn't opened until paragraph 12, and the Rat is still waiting then.

options.text: He tells the Mole to hurry up because his tummy is rumbling loudly.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 11 says he "strove to conceal it". He never tells the Mole he's hungry.

options.text: tummy rumbling loudly
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the clue too. Clue check: nobody hears his tummy. Look at what the Rat says instead.

questions.q: The Mole speaks *with a touch of pride in his manner*. Why is he proud?

options.text: The singers never miss Mole End; they save it till last.
options.why: Clue: "they never pass me over, they come to Mole End last of all". Being saved till last is special.

options.text: He touches the Rat's arm to show off his lovely new coat.
options.why: Clue check: a touch of pride means a little bit of pride. Nobody touches anyone.

options.text: He is proud because he taught the field-mice every carol.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 16 says the carols were "handed down" from their forefathers, not taught by the Mole.

options.text: never missed out
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Which word best describes the Rat tonight, and what is your proof?

options.text: Cheerful: he calls the house capital and makes a jolly fire.
options.why: Clue: "What a capital little house this is!" he called out cheerily, and soon had "a cheerful blaze".

options.text: Grumpy: he moans that the Mole's house is far too small and dusty.
options.why: Clue check: it's the Mole who moans in paragraph 2. The Rat says "So compact!"

options.text: Lazy: he sits by the fire while the Mole does all of the work.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 4 the Rat is "running to and fro with armfuls of fuel".

options.text: Greedy: he eats the whole German sausage before the Mole can.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 11 the Rat is hungry but waits. Nobody has eaten yet.

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: At his door as the field-mice start a carol, proud and happy.
options.why: Clue: the field-mice stand in a semicircle and "their shrill little voices uprose on the air". Mole said "It will be like old times".

options.text: Tucked in his bunk at Mole End, fast asleep after a long, tiring day.
options.why: Clue check: nobody has gone to bed yet. They haven't even had supper.

options.text: At the table, sad because the field-mice ate all of the sardines.
options.why: Clue check: the field-mice are outside singing. They haven't touched any food.

options.text: cross and cold
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 14 the Mole says "It will be like old times". Does that sound cross?

hints: Mole has nothing to feed the singers, so the Rat sends a field-mouse to the shops for food.
The field-mice are freezing, so the Mole invites them in by the fire to warm up.
The carol singers forget the words, but the Rat helps them until they reach the end.
The sardine tin won't open, so the Mole bangs it with the garden roller until it pops.

ch5n4.title: Singers at the door

questions.q: The carol says *Blowing fingers and stamping feet*. Why are the singers doing that?

options.text: They are trying to warm up, standing out in the cold.
options.why: Clue: the same verse starts "Here we stand in the cold and the sleet". Blowing on fingers and stamping keeps you warm.

options.text: They are blowing kisses and stamping because they are cross.
options.why: Clue check: the verse says they have come "you to greet" and bid "joy". They aren't cross.

options.text: It is a dance they do at the end of every single carol.
options.why: Clue check: look at the line just before it: "in the cold and the sleet". It's about the weather, not a dance.

options.text: they're cold
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How do we know it is a very special night, just as the singing ends?

options.text: Far away, bells ring a joyful peal down the tunnel.
options.why: Clue: "the sound of distant bells ringing a joyful and clangorous peal". Bells ring out for special days like Christmas.

options.text: Snow starts falling inside the house and covers the table.
options.why: Clue check: nothing falls inside. Paragraph 7 is about a sound they hear.

options.text: An owl hoots three times from the top of the chimney.
options.why: Clue check: there are no owls tonight. Read what comes "down the tunnel" in paragraph 7.

options.text: an owl hoots
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 7 says the sound is "a faint musical hum" from far away. What makes that sound?

questions.q: The Rat invites the singers in for something hot. Why does the Mole suddenly nearly cry?

options.text: He remembers he has no food or drink to give them.
options.why: Clue: "Whatever are we doing? We've nothing to give them!"

options.text: He is sad the carol is over and wishes it went on longer.
options.why: Clue check: he says "This is quite like old times!" and is happy, until he remembers something.

options.text: The field-mice tread snow all over his nice clean floor.
options.why: Clue check: read what the Mole cries out in paragraph 9. It's not about the floor.

options.text: nothing to give
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The storyteller calls him *the masterful Rat*. What does that show?

options.text: He takes charge and knows just how to fix the problem.
options.why: Clue: he says "You leave all that to me" and straight away asks about the shops.

options.text: The Rat is master of the house, so the Mole must obey him.
options.why: Clue check: it's the Mole's house, not the Rat's. Masterful here means good at taking charge.

options.text: The Rat is a school master who teaches the field-mice to sing.
options.why: Clue check: the field-mice sang before the Rat said a word. He isn't their teacher.

options.text: takes charge
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How can we tell the Rat is fussy about the food he orders?

options.text: He wants only fresh, home-made things, and only the best.
options.why: Clue: "Fresh, mind!", "only the best" and "home-made, no tinned stuff".

options.text: He tells the mouse to buy whatever is cheapest in the shop.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 13 the Rat says "only the best". That's not the cheapest.

options.text: He writes a very long list and makes the mouse learn it.
options.why: Clue check: nobody writes anything. The Mole only hears "bits" of their muttered talk.

options.text: cheapest is best
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 13 says "only the best" and "no tinned stuff".

questions.q: Why can't the field-mouse act his part in last year's play?

options.text: He gets stage-fright and is too shy to say a single word.
options.why: Clue: he "giggled shyly... and remained absolutely tongue-tied" and "nothing could overcome his stage-fright".

options.text: He has a sore throat from singing so many carols in the cold.
options.why: Clue check: nobody says his throat hurts. Paragraph 18 names the real problem.

options.text: He has forgotten all the words, because the play was last year.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 18 blames "his stage-fright", not his memory.

options.text: too shy
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Mole eats *the provender so magically provided*. Why does the storyteller say magically?

options.text: The table was bare, then suddenly it was full of food.
options.why: Clue: "a lately barren board set thick with savoury comforts". Empty one minute, full the next, like magic!

options.text: The Rat is a wizard and makes all the food with a spell.
options.why: Clue check: the food came in the field-mouse's basket from the shops. No spells!

options.text: A fairy flew in through the window with a basket of cakes.
options.why: Clue check: it was the field-mouse with the lantern who came back with the basket in paragraph 18.

options.text: empty to full
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: When the Mole first got home, he was ashamed of his house. How does he feel about it by the very end?

options.text: It's plain and small, but it's all his and he's glad to have it.
options.why: Clue: he saw "how plain and simple" it was, "but clearly, too, how much it all meant to him".

options.text: He wants to stay there forever and never go back up to the river.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 22 says "he knew he must return to the larger stage". He will go back.

options.text: He is still ashamed of it and plans to sell it to the field-mice.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 22 says the old room "smilingly received him back". He isn't ashamed any more.

options.text: still ashamed
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 22 he has his head on his pillow "in great joy and contentment".

questions.q: Which word best describes how the Rat treats the Mole tonight, and what is your proof?

options.text: Thoughtful: he quietly makes sure the Mole has no worries at all.
options.why: Clue: the Rat said little, "only taking care... that Mole had no trouble or anxiety about anything".

options.text: Bossy: he makes the Mole do all the cooking and all the washing up.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 19 the Rat sets everybody to work, and the Mole sits at the head of the table.

options.text: Show-off: he tells the field-mice he paid for the whole feast.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 19 says the Rat "said little or nothing".

options.text: Sleepy: he goes to bed before the singers have even had supper.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat only goes to bed after the field-mice have "clattered off at last".

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: In his bunk at Mole End, happy and at peace with his old home.
options.why: Clue: "soon had his head on his pillow, in great joy and contentment".

options.text: Walking back to the river bank, sad to leave his home once again.
options.why: Clue check: in the last paragraph he is in bed at Mole End. Nobody is walking anywhere.

options.text: By the fire with the field-mice, still waiting for the food to come.
options.why: Clue check: the food came and was eaten, and the field-mice "clattered off at last".

options.text: at River Bank
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: the last paragraph calls it "his old room". Which house is that?

hints: Toad buys yet another motor-car, so Badger, Rat and Mole march to Toad Hall to stop him.
The Rat misses his river, but the Mole walks him home in the morning until he is happy again.
The field-mice come back hungry for breakfast, but the food is gone, so they sing for their porridge.
Snow blocks the tunnel out of Mole End, so the Mole digs a new way up to the fields.
